newsitem.title: USA: Stocks tumble on H-P earnings, rate worries.
newsitem.headline: Stocks tumble on H-P earnings, rate worries.

text.p: Stocks tumbled Friday, led by a sell-off in Hewlett-Packard Co. shares, as surprisingly strong economic news revived fears that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next week.

The Dow Jones industrial average fell 138.88 points, or 1.89 percent, to 7,194.67. For the week it was up 25.14 points. In the broader market, declining issues outpaced gainers, 1,432-979, on volume of 485.8 million on the New York Stock Exchange.

The interest rate jitters started boiling after the government reported that housing starts rose by a stronger-than-expected 2.6 percent in April. Profit-taking and volatility from options trading also fuelled the losses.
"We have a market that has come a very long way in a short period of time and is vulnerable to some normal profit-taking," said Alfred Goldman, technical analyst at A.G. Edwards & Sons.
The Dow has climbed about 940 points from its close at 6,392 on April 11 to Thursday's record close of 7,333.55.
Goldman said the stock market also had to contend with a "double witching" expiration of individual and index options Friday, which often leads to volatility in the stock market.
Asked if a hike in short-term interest rates is possible at the Fed's meeting on Tuesday, Goldman said, "My gut feeling is that they will."
But Wall Street will get over it quickly, he added. "The market will be negative for about half a day and that will be about it. It's still a bull market."

Jeffrey Applegate, chief investment strategist at Lehman Bros., said stocks also retreated on the housing figures and a survey showing consumers in a more buoyant mood. In addition, he said a weak bond market and sell programmes tied to the double expirations exacerbated the decline.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury fell 15/32, pushing the yield to 6.91 percent from 6.87 percent at Thursday's close. Prices and yields move in opposite directions.
Applegate said stocks and bonds were locked in such a narrow range that it is all but impossible for stocks to go if bonds fell.
Hugh Johnson at First Albany Corp. predicted the Fed will stand pat on Tuesday, arguing that a shift in the economy will persuade the central bankers not to make a move.
Although the housing starts were an exception, he said "the economic numbers for the second quarter have suggested fairly clearly that the economy is slowing."
As for the direction of the stock market, Johnson expects "a very sharp correction" which will be healthy.

Hewlett-Packard fell 6-1/8 to 52-3/4, a day after the company reported second-quarter earnings that fell below Wall Street estimates. While the earnings were up from a year ago, analyst Monika Eraiba of Gruntal & Co/ said the biggest problem in the latest quarter was a revenue shortfall.
VeriFone Inc. tumbled 6-1/2 to 51. Last month, VeriFone agreed to be acquired by Heweltt-Packard in a one-for-one stock exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite index slid 12.85 points to 1,340.73, for a gain of 5.68 on the week.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 12.13 points to 829.75 but was up 4.97 from last Friday. The American Stock Exchange index rose 3.25 to 586.72, up 12.94 on the week.
The NYSE composite index of all listed common stocks fell 5.21 to 432.44, but it rose 3.21 from last Friday. The average price per share fell 51 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,832.406, down 91.837 or 1.16 percent. The index was up 51.294 on the week.
